items.title: What Universities Say They Are For
items.researchQuestion: How has the public language universities use to describe their purpose changed over time?
items.firstRunnableBuild: Run current-page fetch, Wayback snapshot fetch, report build, audit packet, and readiness gate.
items.publicationAngle: A longitudinal essay about the movement from truth/civic language toward innovation, impact, global, and inclusion language, with careful source-layer caveats.
qualityRisks: Wayback coverage is sparse for exact current URLs
mission pages move or split across about/value/strategic-plan pages
short archived pages can produce false term drift

items.title: The Rise Of AI And The Humanities
items.researchQuestion: What are scholars publishing about AI, computation, archives, and quantitative methods in humanities-facing fields?
nextSources: JSTOR Data for Research where permitted
items.firstRunnableBuild: Run humanities literature radar pipeline with broad 2020-present source limits, normalize works, build report, and run readiness gate.
items.publicationAngle: A field-map essay showing where AI and quantitative methods are already entering humanities work, what corpora are being used, and which study directions look underexplored.
qualityRisks: metadata coverage underrepresents books and chapters
recent-year indexing lag can look like intellectual decline
keyword searches can overrepresent AI-explicit work and miss implicit computational methods

items.title: The Language Of Museums After Decolonization
items.researchQuestion: How have museums changed public language around civilization, world culture, provenance, restitution, repatriation, and decolonization?
items.unitOfAnalysis: museum page or annual-report section snapshot
nextSources: exhibition catalogs where metadata is public
items.firstRunnableBuild: Current-page source probe exists for 33 pages across 14 museums and five source genres; sparse Wayback coverage exists for 4 historical snapshots in the latest run. Next build should add provenance, annual-report, and historically stable URL source layers.
items.publicationAngle: A longitudinal institutional-language essay about how museums publicly explain ownership, culture, world history, and repair.
qualityRisks: page redesigns can change text independently of institutional ideology
annual reports and exhibition pages represent different genres
some museums expose rich collection APIs while others expose only web copy

items.title: Canon Drift: A Feasibility Report
items.researchQuestion: Which sources can credibly measure changes in assigned, anthologized, cited, translated, or held authors over time?
items.unitOfAnalysis: author-work appearance in a syllabus, anthology, citation graph, translation record, or library-holdings record
items.firstRunnableBuild: Source-probe pipeline exists for public courseware, Open Syllabus, anthology/publisher pages, Library of Congress JSON, library catalogs, and OpenAlex author searches. Latest run produced 13 probes, 11 accessible probes, and 5 signal types.
items.publicationAngle: A methods-forward public essay explaining what canon drift can and cannot be measured from public data before making large claims.
qualityRisks: syllabi are not a representative sample of teaching
library holdings measure acquisition and preservation, not readership
anthology editions require careful edition-level normalization

items.title: What Counts As A Humanities Dataset?
items.researchQuestion: What reusable corpora could support new quantitative humanities essays, and which are ready for immediate analysis?
items.firstRunnableBuild: Dataset registry pipeline exists for 15 candidate corpora across museum collections, books, newspapers, archives, linked data, repositories, and syllabi. Latest run produced 11 accessible candidates, 6 ready-now candidates, and 5 generated study specs.
items.publicationAngle: A practical field guide to humanities datasets that can become public essays, not just academic infrastructure.
qualityRisks: dataset descriptions often overstate completeness
licenses may allow inspection but not republication
corpora may require domain-specific normalization before they are analytically useful

items.title: When Museums Started Explaining Repair
items.researchQuestion: How did museum annual reports and public accountability documents change their language around provenance, restitution, repatriation, access, and community between 2000 and 2026?
items.unitOfAnalysis: museum annual report section or paragraph snapshot
primarySources: Internet Archive snapshots for report indexes
nextSources: exhibition catalogs where metadata is public
items.firstRunnableBuild: Select 12 museums already present in museum-language-drift, fetch all public annual reports available for 2000-2026, extract text into paragraph records, and reuse the existing museum term taxonomy with a document-genre label.
items.publicationAngle: A follow-up to the museum language post: not just what museums say on web pages, but when repair and accountability entered their institutional record.
items.publishableEvidence: Broad backfill, raw manifests, processed records, and representative audited snippets tied to every major claim.
qualityRisks: annual reports may be written for donors rather than public interpretation
PDF availability may be uneven by museum and year
report design and OCR quality may create artificial language shifts

items.title: The Strategic Plan University
items.researchQuestion: Do university strategic plans show a stronger shift toward innovation, impact, global leadership, belonging, and workforce language than mission/about pages?
primarySources: Internet Archive snapshots of plan pages
items.firstRunnableBuild: Use the 10 universities in university-mission-statement-drift, collect public strategic plans and president messages for 2000, 2010, 2015, 2020, and 2026 anchors, then compare against existing mission-page term families.
items.publicationAngle: Universities may not have changed what they say they are for as much as how they plan, manage, and justify themselves.
items.publishableEvidence: Broad backfill, raw manifests, processed records, and representative audited snippets tied to every major claim.
qualityRisks: strategic plans may be episodic and not comparable year by year
universities may remove old plans from public sites
consultant-written plans can converge stylistically without reflecting institutional purpose

items.title: What Humanities AI Actually Studies
items.researchQuestion: Which corpora, archives, languages, periods, and media types appear most often in AI-for-humanities work from 2020 onward?
items.unitOfAnalysis: scholarly work to named corpus/archive/dataset mention
primarySources: paper full text where open and permitted
items.firstRunnableBuild: Start from the 593 quantitative/computational candidates in humanities-literature-radar, extract corpus/entity mentions from titles and abstracts, then audit the top 100 mentions before scaling to open full text.
items.publicationAngle: AI in the humanities is not only a method trend; it is a map of which parts of culture are becoming computationally visible.
items.publishableEvidence: Audited top corpus mentions with source links and false-positive estimates.
qualityRisks: metadata abstracts may omit corpus names
full-text access may bias toward open preprints
named entity extraction can merge projects, datasets, and institutions incorrectly

items.title: The Anthology Table Of Contents As Canon Sensor
items.researchQuestion: Can public anthology tables of contents and publisher previews measure author and work turnover across editions in a narrow literary field?
items.unitOfAnalysis: author-work appearance in an anthology edition table of contents
primarySources: Google Books snippets where permitted for bibliographic metadata
items.firstRunnableBuild: Pick one anthology family with public TOC evidence across at least three editions, build an edition-level table, and compare against a small public syllabus control set without treating syllabi as representative.
items.publicationAngle: Canon drift becomes measurable only when the source is narrow enough to audit edition by edition.
items.publishableEvidence: At least three editions with auditable TOC rows, edition-year metadata, and explicit missing-source notes.
qualityRisks: tables of contents may be copyrighted or not publicly extractable at scale
anthologies differ in market and course level
edition changes can reflect permissions and price rather than canon judgment

items.title: The Afterlife Of Humanities Datasets
items.researchQuestion: What happens to public humanities datasets after release: do they get cited, forked, reused in papers, linked from projects, or quietly disappear?
nextSources: repository issue and release metadata where public
items.firstRunnableBuild: Take the 15 dataset-registry candidates, collect DOI/URL/repository identifiers, query OpenAlex and repository metadata for reuse signals, and hand-audit the top and bottom cases.
items.publicationAngle: Humanities datasets are infrastructure, but their public afterlife is uneven and measurable.
items.publishableEvidence: Broad backfill, raw manifests, processed records, and representative audited snippets tied to every major claim.
qualityRisks: reuse is often informal and hard to observe
citations may attach to papers rather than datasets
older datasets may predate modern DOI and repository practices
